Amazon logistics automation offers long-term margin gains, Jefferies says Proactive uses images sourced from Shutterstock

Amazon.com Inc (NASDAQ:AMZN) could strengthen its retail margins through warehouse automation and an expanding logistics network, as investments in fulfillment capacity and third-party parcel delivery create new opportunities, according to Jefferies.

Following a discussion with a logistics industry expert, the broker said automation remains a key long-term competitive advantage for Amazon, helping reduce its exposure to labour shortages and wage inflation even if immediate cost savings prove limited.

Amazon has deployed more than 1 million robots, but the expert estimates only 40% to 45% of its US small-sortable fulfillment centers are highly automated, suggesting considerable room for further adoption.

Newer facilities can process around 1 million units on peak days with approximately 1,000 workers, compared with 2,500 to 3,000 historically. A US$1 hourly increase in warehouse and driver wages would add an estimated US$1.1 billion to operating expenses, highlighting the value of reducing labor dependency.

Jefferies also sees renewed investment in retail logistics, with gross logistics space additions rising from 56 million square feet in 2025 to 81 million in 2026. Amazon has around US$27 billion in visible capital expenditure planned over the next couple of years, covering automated fulfillment centers, inbound cross-docks and delivery infrastructure.

The broker identified third-party parcel delivery as another potential growth area. Amazon could expand its US delivery stations from approximately 575 to 950 by 2030, allowing it to handle more shipments currently managed by UPS and the US Postal Service.

Early trials reportedly show 20% to 25% savings for business-to-consumer shippers, partly because Amazon avoids some residential, weekend and package surcharges charged by established carriers. However, execution during peak shopping periods remains a key test.

Grocery presents a more difficult challenge. Delivery costs of US$10 to US$12 per order make smaller baskets challenging to profitably serve.

Jefferies sees potential in Amazon's planned Illinois hybrid retail and fulfillment concept, expected in 2028, which would combine large-format shopping with automated rapid delivery.

The broker remains constructive on Amazon's margin outlook, expecting fulfillment efficiencies and AWS operating leverage to offset the structural challenges of its retail business.

title: Amazon or Alphabet: If I Could Only Own One for the Next Decade, It Would Be This One

Amazon or Alphabet: If I Could Only Own One for the Next Decade, It Would Be This One
Prosper Junior Bakiny, The Motley Fool

Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) and Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL) are two companies that hardly need an introduction. Both are leaders in their respective industries, generally post excellent financial results, and have crushed broader equities over the long run. Investors arguably can't go wrong with either of these, and I personally own shares of both. But if I had to pick just one to own for the next decade, it would likely be Alphabet. Here's why.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The AI tailwind could favor Alphabet

Over the next 10 years, the cloud computing and artificial intelligence (AI) industries will likely continue growing. Amazon and Alphabet, two leaders in these markets, are both likely to capitalize. What separates the two companies? Let's start with Amazon. The company's cloud segment, Amazon Web Services (AWS), boasts the largest market share.

Amazon offers perhaps the largest library of services among the Big Three in the cloud computing industry. However, Alphabet is particularly competitive in the AI niche of the cloud market. Alphabet's cloud sales have been growing faster in recent quarters. During the second quarter, Google Cloud's revenue soared by 82% year over year to $24.8 billion. Alphabet's total revenue jumped by 24% year over year to $119.8 billion.

By contrast, Amazon's total revenue increased 20% year over year to $200.6 billion, with AWS cloud sales jumping 37% year over year to $42.2 billion. One reason I'd pick Alphabet over Amazon right now is the former's strength in AI. Despite fears that the AI bubble will burst, spending on the technology continues to rise, and we are arguably just entering the era of agentic AI systems.

There is at least some evidence that demand for agentic AI is there. Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) launched one of the first consumer-facing AI agents in September, and it has been hugely successful so far. Corporations are also extensively using AI agents. And as more of them are developed, demand for precisely the sort of services that Alphabet and Amazon offer should continue to rise. All that to say, bullish long-term projections about AI infrastructure spending appear justified, and Alphabet is in a particularly strong position to capitalize on that.

Margins matter

What if we look at the rest of their businesses? Amazon's is larger, at least in terms of sales. But Alphabet has an advantage. Its business carries much higher margins. That's not surprising. Alphabet makes most of its money from digital ads (Amazon's ad business is much smaller than Alphabet's). Once the advertising infrastructure is up and running, the cost of showing one additional ad is small. Meanwhile, Amazon's core e-commerce business is a famously low-margin operation.

According to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, Steve Ballmer, banished from the NBA for bad behavior, was pushed out as Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) CEO in 2014 and is the world's 7th-richest person, with a net worth of $186 billion. His former boss, Bill Gates, ranks 17th at $119 billion (maybe because of his 2021 divorce).

Satya Nadella replaced Ballmer as CEO. Nadella had held the CEO job for a decade. The stock had performed poorly under Ballmer. He missed the smartphone revolution. He missed the early stages of cloud computing.

Microsoft Sweden, via Wikimedia Commons

Some people thought Ballmer was made CEO because of a friendship he had with Gates at Harvard that stretched back to 1976. In 1980, Ballmer became Microsoft's 30th employee and served as Bill Gates's primary lieutenant until he moved upstairs as Gates stepped down as CEO.

Ballmer did not get mad. He got even. Since 1986, Microsoft shares are up 520,000%. Ballmer owns 4.2% of the company.

title: UPS Volume Is Still Falling. Does Better Pricing Make Up For It?

UPS Volume Is Still Falling. Does Better Pricing Make Up For It?

Shares of United Parcel Service (UPS) trade at 18.3 times earnings, compared with 23.0 for the S&P 500. Investors paying that price need to understand what they are buying, and the company's priorities have changed. During the fiscal Q2 2025 earnings call in July 2025, management reported a 7.3% drop in the number of packages UPS handled each day in the U.S. Executives reported an 8% decline on the April 2026 call. On the July 2026 call, management said the decline had narrowed to 3.3% as the planned cut in Amazon volume ended. So what else is management stressing?

UPS Now Talks Up Its Revenue Per Package

Management now emphasizes revenue per piece, which measures the amount UPS earns on each package. During the fiscal Q2 2026 call in July, executives said this metric rose 9.3% from a year earlier. Base rates and a better customer mix drove more than half of that increase, management said, with fuel making up the rest.

Daily package counts mattered while UPS reshaped its network. Management said on the fiscal Q1 2025 call that the company was executing the largest network reconfiguration in its history. By the fiscal Q2 2026 call, executives said UPS had eliminated about 2 million pieces per day of lower-quality Amazon volume.

In fiscal Q2 2026, higher revenue per package came with higher overall sales. That did not happen in fiscal Q1 2026, when revenue fell 1.6% even as revenue per package rose 6.5%. UPS generated $22.8 billion in revenue during fiscal Q2 2026, up 7.6% from a year earlier. Over the past twelve months, however, revenue was 0.4% lower than in the twelve months before, so one strong quarter is not yet a trend.

When United Parcel Service is a large share of what you own, what its management stops saying matters more. See how to protect a concentrated position.

How Much Of UPS Do Premium Customers Make Up?

Smaller business customers generated 34.5% of U.S. volume for UPS in fiscal Q2 2026, an increase of 250 basis points from a year earlier. Daily volume for this group grew 4.3%. On the earnings call, management said UPS is fully focused on capturing premium volume from smaller businesses, healthcare and business-to-business customers.

Business-to-business customers represent a larger share, accounting for 43.8% of U.S. volume. Daily volume for these shippers fell 3.2% from a year earlier, a decline 190 basis points smaller than in fiscal Q1 2026. All of these customers operate within a U.S. package business that still forms the bulk of UPS, making up 67.1% of company revenue in fiscal 2025. Revenue for this unit fell 1.4% from fiscal 2024.
